doc.title: Allan Vaché interviewed by Monk Rowe, Scottsdale, Arizona, April 15, 2000

title: Becoming a clarinetist: Goodman, DeFranco and the bop era
summary: Why clarinet players were scarce in the bop era, and his influences from Goodman, DeFranco and Tony Scott.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Who were the great clarinetists? Favorites and rivals

blocks.x: Yeah, pretty much. I mean I spent a lot of time listening to Benny Goodman records, and becoming a clarinetist especially. What’s available to listen to, as opposed to because during the bop era, when bop became real popular, there weren’t too many clarinet players anymore. The clarinet players were Goodman and Shaw and those guys, the guys who led the big bands. But there are a lot more saxophone players because there were five saxophones in every big band, and usually only one clarinet player if any at all. So there were a lot more saxophone players so therefore the saxophone became more of a common instrument. But there were still Buddy DeFranco and Tony Scott and a few other guys who were playing the clarinet and playing it bop, so I’ve been influenced by that but I know a few of those tunes but my sense of improvisation never really gravitated to that style of music, not that I don’t love it, just like I like to listen to a Mozart symphony but I wouldn’t be very good playing it.
